blogs.title: Early progress on accelerating drug development with Claude
blogs.author: Anthropic
blogs.description: Over the past several months, we’ve partnered with six organizations to accelerate curing disease. We’ve also started drug discovery efforts of our own, including programs for rare childhood forms of muscular dystrophy. In this post, we provide an update on our progress.
blogs.content: Chapter 01 : Case studies Anthropic’s life sciences team is working to accelerate curing disease. Over the past several months, our scientists have engaged in deep research partnerships with six organizations developing new medicines: BigHat Biosciences , Bristol Myers Squibb , Divergence Labs , Enveda , Generate Biomedicines , and The Column Group . We've also begun drug discovery efforts of our own. In doing so, we've learned a lot about how Claude can support drug development, and how we’ll need to improve Claude further to realize AI's potential in medicine. We plan to scale this work up substantially from here . There are many opportunities to speed up drug development, even beyond the most commonly discussed applications of AI, like proposing initial designs for new molecules. Developing a drug involves many varied tasks: doing early research to identify a target for a drug and the right type of drug to engage it, designing a molecule with the right properties, optimizing it to be manufactured reliably at scale, drafting the regulatory filings needed to run clinical trials, designing and administering those trials, and much more. Our strategy to realize AI’s medical benefits is based on having AI increasingly involved in all of these tasks. There is no single problem to solve; the bottlenecks are distributed all throughout the drug development process. The best way to identify and work through these bottlenecks is to get deeply involved in real drug programs, across many different disease areas and stages of development. So, over the past several months, we’ve partnered with six organizations to do so. We’ve also started drug discovery efforts of our own, including programs for rare childhood forms of muscular dystrophy, where Claude handles much of the scientific and operational work. This work serves our goals in three ways. First, it lets us better understand the strengths and limitations of our models in relation to a much wider range of drug development tasks (we’ve already prioritized specific improvements to our models based on what we’ve learned so far). Second, these programs can serve as case studies for the wider life sciences community. If Claude is to significantly increase the rate of new cures, we need to work with many more biotechnology firms and integrate Claude more deeply into their development processes. Third, these projects should, if their positive trajectories continue, have direct impact themselves. We’re optimistic that some may result in effective new medicines for the diseases they target, including food allergies, rare childhood diseases, and several forms of cancer. In this post, we provide an update on our progress with our partners, along with technical reports that describe our thought process, methods, and early results in more detail. We then briefly outline where our work is headed next. Case studies Generate Biomedicines: modality engineering. Generate Biomedicines has been working on increasing the usefulness of a cancer treatment known as CAR T-cell therapy. This therapy has historically helped treat blood cell cancers; Generate aims to reengineer it so that it can treat solid tumor cancers too. To do this, they’re aiming to shorten one part of the therapy’s genetic instructions, which would create room for additional instructions suited to other kinds of cancer. Six Generate scientists used Claude Code to propose new designs for this part. One design was about 70% shorter than the standard version, and in lab tests it was more effective: it allowed immune cells to make roughly 10 times as many receptors (the proteins they use to spot cancer cells), it killed tumor cells more efficiently, and the immune cells remained active for longer. Read more , and see Generate’s technical report . Divergence Labs: hit generation. Divergence Labs is working on a novel way to treat food allergies. Food allergies are set off by a reaction from a molecule called IgE, some of which is attached to our immune cells and some of which floats freely in our blood. Divergence Labs is developing drugs that would detach the IgE from our immune cells entirely, rather than solely neutralizing the IgE circulating in our blood, as standard medications do. This could provide a much more effective treatment, but it requires a precise design, with two “arms”: one that would bind tightly to IgE, and another that would help prise IgE from the immune cell. Claude converted Divergence Labs’ goals into a detailed design plan, and then, largely autonomously, generated roughly 35,000 antibody designs in about a month to be narrowed down and tested. In those early tests, Divergence found “hits” for both arms: three designs that could bind to IgE, and 20 that could dislodge it. Three of those 20 appeared to dislodge IgE more than the standard medication. Its next step is to build a drug that combines the two arms. Read more , and see Divergence’s technical report . BigHat Biosciences: lead optimization. BigHat Biosciences pairs AI with an automated lab to improve potential drugs (or “leads”), which must bind their target tightly, remain stable through manufacturing and storage, and avoid clumping together (among other criteria). BigHat’s scientists and an Anthropic researcher worked with Claude to improve these three properties in two leads, both antibody fragments that could become parts of future drugs: one designed to target cancer cells, and one designed to keep a drug in the body longer. Claude, connected to BigHat’s lab data system, Reccy, proposed changes to each molecule, and BigHat’s lab made and tested about 1,010 variants in about 10 weeks. Partway through, the team suspected the standard heat-stability and clumping metrics were misleading. Claude and the researcher reanalyzed the raw data, then proposed different metrics and a protocol change to test them. BigHat’s scientists refined and ran it, and the main predictions held. Compared with the originals, the best versions bound more than 10x more tightly, the cancer-targeting lead stayed in solution 18°C higher, and the lead for longer-lasting drugs clumped more than 100x more slowly. Read more , and see BigHat’s technical report . Enveda: manufacturing and filings. To conduct clinical trials, companies need records showing that each batch of a new drug has been made to strict quality standards, and to submit an application to regulators, among other requirements. At Enveda, manufacturing chemists spent up to 75% of their time on paperwork. To ease the load, Enveda built a system that connects all of its manufacturing documents to Claude, then lets Claude flag any possible issues. Over tests on 1,061 pages of documentation, Claude caught all 11 issues that human reviewers had spotted—and flagged seven they’d missed. In the process, this method reduced human review time by 89%, from over 25 hours to less than three. Separately, Claude wrote the first drafts of two important regulatory documents. One took four hours, compared to about three months by hand. For the other, Enveda’s standard human review process found one minor error. Read more , and see Enveda’s technical report . The Column Group (TCG): company creation. Because drug discovery can be slow, expensive, and prone to failure, investors in biotechnology companies have favored safer, previously validated ideas over riskier new ones, even when the latter could help more patients. We’ve been working with TCG to see whether Claude can change this by cutting the time and cost of drug discovery so that investors can confidently support more ambitious ideas. Specifically, TCG is establishing Pleiades, a new company that will use Claude to run many more—and more complex—drug programs than is usual for a small team. This could be a model for how Claude can reduce both the scientific and the operational and administrative overhead required to run a biotechnology company. If this works, this model could be replicated across the industry and direct investment toward harder problems in medicine. Pleiades is currently developing new tools and workflows for Claude; its very first Claude skill, which helps Claude assess whether drug targets are worth pursuing, has been evaluated on 45 target-disease pairs. Read more . More recently, we’ve also begun working with Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS) to find and address bottlenecks in clinical trial planning. BMS is using Claude to assess plans of an early-stage drug in clinical trials, and to estimate the likelihood of those trials succeeding. Together, we plan to expand this work in 2027 to understand its potential for increasing the probability of success in early development. “We use Claude at the clinical trial stage to analyze proprietary data, create a clinical study plan, and weigh the study’s chance of success. From a single prompt, Claude generated a robust initial analysis that helped inform our assessment of different development options, which would otherwise take days to complete. We did all of this while ensuring the security of our highly sensitive data. We look forward to expanding this work across our pipeline to support portfolio-level decisions.” Michael Pourdehnad, MD , Senior Vice President, Head of Early Clinical Development, Hematology, Oncology and Cell Therapy. In addition to our work with these partners, we’ve begun to run some research programs ourselves. We’ve acquired Mithril Medicine, a one-person company that has been developing treatments for two rare forms of muscular dystrophy. Its founder, Cody Tranbarger, used Claude to organize contracts, logistics, and experiments with 11 external labs, and delegated many other aspects of Mithril’s operations to Claude. As a result, Mithril took a possible treatment for one form of muscular dystrophy from an idea to promising results in mice in less than 18 months. Now at Anthropic, Cody is continuing this research, and plans to start several new programs. If his drug candidates continue to hold up, we expect a drug to be ready to start clinical trials in humans as soon as late 2028. Read more and see our technical report . Extending our work in the life sciences All of this research is still at an early stage. In particular, so far it is mostly preclinical— that is, for the most part, it isn’t yet at the stage where the drugs are being tested in humans. We plan to continue extending Claude’s role into clinical trials as these drug programs advance, and as we partner with more organizations whose drug development programs are already at the clinical stage. This research is only one part of our efforts to accelerate drug discovery. Ultimately, we want to share our models with as many drug development researchers as possible. To that end, we’ve rolled out Claude Science , our AI workbench for researchers, and we’re providing Claude credits for life scientists . We’ve also created the Life Sciences Verification Program to allow trusted organizations to use our most powerful models with more permissive versions of our safeguards, which are necessary to prevent misuse but which can impede legitimate biological research. We’ve also recently launched an open call for guest investigators in the life sciences; we’re seeking proposals from research groups who want to use Claude to investigate key questions in drug discovery and other areas. We’re looking forward to working with many more organizations as we expand our life sciences research. If you work at an organization focused on drug discovery and are interested in collaborating with us, you can get in touch below. Get in touch with us If you work at an organization focused on drug development and would like to get in touch, complete the following form.

blogs.title: The sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning
blogs.content: The sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning October 27, 2026 Ali Behrouz and Vahab Mirrokni, Google Research We introduce a sleep phase in continual learning, enabling large language models to continuously integrate new facts and enhance reasoning while mitigating catastrophic forgetting or static knowledge cutoffs. Modern LLMs achieve impressive performance via pre-training and in-context learning (ICL). However, once deployed, they remain largely static, operating with a fixed knowledge cutoff date that leaves them unable to acquire long-term capabilities or adapt to new information. While updating models with new data seems like the obvious solution, continual parameter updates often trigger catastrophic forgetting , a fundamental issue where learning new tasks severely degrades performance on previously learned ones. Alternatively, relying strictly on ICL limits knowledge retention to the immediate context window: once the context session ends, the acquired short-term information is forgotten. Inspired by how the human brain processes and stabilizes memory during rest, we introduce a sleep framework in continual learning: a learning paradigm that equips large language models (LLMs) with a continuous periodic lifecycle, enabling them to continually learn, consolidate fragile short-term context into stable long-term parameters. With this framework, we demonstrate that alternating between active interaction and offline memory consolidation allows LLMs to continuously acquire new facts, retain long-context knowledge up to 10M tokens, and improve complex reasoning. Rethinking machine learning: Active (wake) vs. sleep phases Traditional machine learning relies on a strict separation between training and inference. In a continual learning framework, this distinction becomes artificial; an intelligent agent must constantly learn, adapt, and process information. Under the sleep paradigm, an LLM operates across two primary states: Active (wake) phase : The model actively receives, processes, and interacts with inputs, storing temporary information in fast, short-term memory components. Sleep phase : The model pauses processing new inputs and redirects its internal computations toward memory consolidation and self-improvement. While terms like "sleep," "dreaming," and "self-improvement" borrow from neuroscience, our framework operates entirely within a fixed model architecture and human-defined training rules. During the offline sleep phase, the model unlocks pre-allocated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) memory blocks and updates its numerical weights using self-generated practice examples. This automated post-training cycle helps a deployed model absorb new facts and sharpen its reasoning accuracy while keeping its core codebase and design unchanged. Key components of the sleep process The sleep paradigm addresses catastrophic forgetting and continuous adaptation through two stages: memory consolidation and dreaming. 1. Memory consolidation In the human brain, non-rapid eye movement (NREM) slow-wave sleep consolidates fragile memories into long-term structures via abstraction and distillation. Our proposed sleep framework mirrors this natural phenomenon through two key technical mechanisms: Parameter expansion & continuum memory hierarchy: To prevent catastrophic forgetting, the model dynamically scales its capacity during sleep. Using a Mixture of Experts (MoE) and Hope architecture , newly unlocked, low-rank experts are integrated into stable, lower-frequency memory blocks to store incoming knowledge without disrupting older parameters. Knowledge seeding (upward distillation): Fragile short-term memories stored in high-frequency layers (e.g., in-context memory) are transferred into the newly expanded long-term parameters. This is achieved through Generalized Knowledge Distillation (GKD) combined with reinforcement learning (RL)-based imitation learning : On-policy distillation: The expanded student model learns token-specific feedback from teacher distributions generated on self-sampled sequences. Learning to imitate (LTI): The student model is rewarded based on semantic and absolute similarity ( Levenshtein distance ) when completing prefixes of teacher-generated text. Synaptic pruning: Once the memory consolidation into lower-frequency modules is complete, the high-frequency temporary parameters are reset, freeing up capacity for future active sessions. Overview of our sleep framework: Input streams from the active phase are stored in short-term memory before entering the sleep cycle, which bifurcates into Consolidation (transferring fragile short-term tokens into expanded long-term parametric memory using low-rank structures and MoE) and Dreaming (autonomous self-improvement via synthetic routing with random experts and RL refinement). 2. Dreaming for self-improvement During REM sleep , the human brain actively simulates scenarios, consolidates emotional/semantic connections, and explores novel neural pathways. Mirroring this, during the “dreaming stage”, the sleep framework implements an autonomous self-improvement loop: Random expert selection: During synthetic data generation, the MoE router randomly activates non-standard experts. This forces the model to mix disparate domains of knowledge and uncover latent patterns. Curated rehearsal: The model generates synthetic training samples ("dreams") and filters them using gradient-based data selection to prioritize samples with the highest potential to boost overall model capability. RL refinement: The model performs supervised fine-tuning on top-rated dream samples and evaluates whether the generation improves performance on downstream tasks. Theoretical foundations Beyond the empirical results, our sleep paradigm is grounded in a theory that clarifies why its two stages (memory consolidation and dreaming) can support continual learning without simply trading new knowledge for old capabilities. For memory consolidation, the analysis shows that knowledge seeding can be understood as a structured, low-rank compression problem. The model is not asked to copy every detail of its short-term traces into its parameters. Instead, it identifies a compact set of directions that best preserve both the model’s own on-policy behavior and the semantic qualities rewarded by the learning objective. This perspective explains the complementary roles of the two signals: on-policy distillation aligns consolidation with the trajectories the model will actually produce at inference time, reducing the mismatch that can arise when training only on teacher-generated distributions; meanwhile, the semantic reward changes what is worth retaining, prioritizing directions that preserve meaning and task-relevant behavior rather than merely matching token probabilities. Parameter expansion then provides the capacity needed to write these selected memories without overwriting previously consolidated knowledge. For dreaming, the theory characterizes random expert activation and reward-based sample selection as mechanisms for improving the geometry of learning. Injecting different MoEs broadens the set of gradient directions explored during synthetic generation, exposing the model to a richer collection of updates than those induced by its ordinary wake-time data alone. Gradient-based filtering then emphasizes the synthetic experiences that carry the most useful learning signal, strengthening informative directions while preserving the structure of the underlying gradient space. Together, these steps yield a more balanced optimization landscape: learning is less dominated by a small number of directions, gradients are better conditioned, and the model can make more stable progress when refining its capabilities. In this view, dreaming is not simply self-generated data augmentation; it is a deliberate process for diversifying, selecting, and consolidating the updates through which the model improves itself. Comparative performance of our sleep framework against baseline approaches (such as in-context learning and supervised fine-tuning) across major evaluation axes, including Class-Incremental Learning, continual translation, long-context scaling up to 10M tokens, factual knowledge incorporation, and mathematical reasoning. For continual translation , in unseen languages, such as Manchu and Kalamang, the sleep framework maintained a near-zero performance drop in multi-stage evaluations, whereas standard baselines like ICL, Cartridges , and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) suffered severe catastrophic forgetting during sequential learning. In long-context understanding on the BABILong benchmark, our sleep method demonstrated near-perfect scaling up to 10M tokens, outperforming strong baselines like GPT-4 , and Titans by using sleep-time consolidation to compress long-context information directly into parametric memory. For factual knowledge incorporation evaluated on SQuAD and continued pre-training (CPT), our sleep method achieved 48.9% on single-task and 46.2% on CPT evaluations, outperforming baseline methods including the base model, SFT, and Self-Adapting Language Models (SEAL) by successfully integrating new factual information without degrading existing model representations. Finally, on mathematical reasoning benchmarks including AIME 24/25 and HMMT 25 , sleep-enhanced base-model achieved accuracy scores of 79.2%, 69.0%, and 46.1%, respectively. This outperformed baselines like SFT, group relative policy optimization (GRPO), and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), showing that pairing memory consolidation with imitation learning drives superior reasoning performance. Conclusion Our sleep paradigm provides a path toward autonomous, continually learning AI systems. By moving beyond static pre-training and fragile context windows, alternating between active learning and offline rest empowers LLMs to retain short-term memories, abstract new skills into long-term parameter structures, and continuously self-improve without catastrophic forgetting. Acknowledgements This research was conducted by Ali Behrouz (Google and Cornell University), Farnoosh Hashemi (Cornell University), Adel Javanmard (Google and University of Southern California), and Vahab Mirrokni. We thank Yuan Deng and Corinna Cortes for reviewing the work and their valuable suggestions. We also thank Mark Simborg, Kimberly Schwede, and Tim Herrmann for their help in crafting this blog post. blogs.title: IBM and Kaggle launch leaderboard for Java framework migration
blogs.author: Bridget McGinn, Raju Pavuluri, Advait Pavuluri, Rahul Krishna, Srikanth Tamilselvam, Ashita Saxena, George Safta, Michele Merler
blogs.description: ScarfBench evaluates model-and-agent-harness combinations for enterprise Java migration, pairing rigorous migration validation with independently reproduced runs and a Kaggle leaderboard.
blogs.content: ScarfBench (Self-Contained Application Refactoring Benchmark) is an open IBM benchmark for evaluating whether coding agents can successfully migrate enterprise Java applications across frameworks while preserving working application behavior. Across Jakarta EE, Quarkus, and Spring migrations, it tests whether generated applications build, start, and continue to behave as expected, using both focused workloads and whole applications Modernizing an enterprise application is not a single-file coding task. Moving an application between frameworks can require coordinated changes to dependency injection, persistence, database access, web endpoints, build systems, framework descriptors, and deployment infrastructure. A coding agent can produce a migration that looks plausible, or even compiles, while the application still fails when deployed or exercised against its expected behavior. ScarfBench asks a practical question: Can an agent take an unfamiliar application, migrate it across framework boundaries, and leave behind software that still works? IBM introduced ScarfBench earlier in 2026 as a reproducible benchmark for AI-driven migrations. Now IBM and Kaggle are partnering to make that evaluation easier to reproduce, compare, and extend over time. Kaggle consulted on the evaluation design, independently reproduced and ran ScarfBench on its platform while sponsoring the compute, and will maintain the benchmark as new models are released. The collaboration turns ScarfBench from a published benchmark into a continuously updated view of progress in agentic software modernization. The original ScarfBench announcement described the benchmark design, developer-verified workloads, and reproducible evaluation approach in detail. This post focuses on what the latest evaluation tells us about model-and-agent-harness combinations, where they fail, and how the benchmark is evolving with Kaggle. Evaluating model-and-harness combinations ScarfBench evaluates an agentic system rather than a language model in isolation. Each result reflects a model paired with a coding-agent harness that determines how it interacts with the repository and development environment. The results should therefore be read as model/harness results, not as measurements of the underlying model alone. Across 204 migration tasks, Gemini 4 Argon with Antigravity ranked first on the primary smoke-test metric at 75.2%, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 with Claude Code at 70.5% and Claude Opus 5 with Claude Code at 69.8%. Ten model-and-harness configurations were evaluated. Rank Model Harness Smoke % All pass % Mean % 1 Gemini 4 Argon Antigravity 75.2 71.1 85.9 2 Claude Opus 5.5 Claude Code 70.5 72.1 82.0 3 Claude Opus 5 Claude Code 69.8 60.8 79.7 4 GPT-6.1 Sol Codex 68.4 62.7 76.8 5 Gemini 3.8 Flash mini-swe 66.0 62.3 77.6 6 GPT-6 Astra Codex 65.4 61.4 75.4 7 Qwen 3.8 Max qwen-code 63.7 59.3 76.1 8 Kimi K3 kimi-code 61.1 50.7 71.2 9 Gemini 3.1 Pro OpenHands 39.5 35.1 50.5 10 Gemma 4 26B-A4B mini-swe 24.5 17.6 30.8 The three metrics reveal an important nuance. The smoke score, the leaderboard metric, awards partial credit and gives larger test suites more weight. On that measure, the Gemini 4 Argon + Antigravity combination had the strongest result. But Claude Opus 5.5 + Claude Code had the highest all-tests-pass rate at 72.1%, narrowly ahead of Gemini 4 Argon. In other words, the Argon/Antigravity combination earned the most partial credit across the benchmark, while the Opus 5.5/Claude Code combination converted slightly more individual migration tasks into completely green test suites. The ranking remains stable under a sensitivity analysis. Four of the 204 migration tasks received zero behavioral-test credit from every evaluated model/harness combination. Excluding those four tasks raised the absolute scores but did not change the ordering at the top: Gemini 4 Argon + Antigravity scored 79.4%, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 + Claude Code at 74.5% and Claude Opus 5 + Claude Code at 73.7%. This result suggests that the relative ranking is not driven by this small set of uniformly difficult tasks. Even the strongest combination leaves substantial headroom: The best overall smoke score was 75.2% across the full benchmark, and no configuration fully passed more than about three-quarters of the migrations. The biggest differentiator is behavioral fidelity, not compilation The clearest result is the gap between code that builds and software that behaves correctly. After excluding the four all-zero tasks, Claude Opus 5 + Claude Code, Gemini 4 Argon + Antigravity and Gemini 3.8 Flash + mini-swe each compiled 100% of tasks, GPT-6 Astra + Codex and Kimi K3 + kimi-code compiled 99.0% and 98.5%, and Claude Opus 5.5 + Claude Code and GPT-6.1 Sol + Codex compiled 98.0% and 98.5%. Yet smoke-test scores remained much lower. Across the 10 configurations, compile success among solvable tasks spanned about 25 percentage points, but most configurations cluster near the top, with 8 of 10 compiling 97% or more; smoke-test performance spanned more than 50 points. Among applications that successfully deployed, the leading configurations clustered at roughly 63 to 76% for fully passing tests; Kimi K3 + kimi-code fell to 53%, Gemini 3.1 Pro + OpenHands to 42%, and Gemma 4 26B-A4B + mini-swe to 26%. In this evaluation, preserving behavior was a much stronger discriminator than getting the migrated application to compile. Where agent configurations fail Of 745 classified failing runs, 535 (approximately 72%) were runtime behavioral failures: The application built and often booted but failed behavioral validation. This group included 304 content or assertion mismatches and 210 lost-route/404 failures; 21 were explicit HTTP 500/405 errors. Compile or packaging failures accounted for roughly 20% (152 runs), and boot or dependency-injection crashes for roughly 8% (58 runs). Lost routes and HTTP semantics: In concurrency-taskcreator-quarkus-to-jakarta, Claude Opus 5 + Claude Code scored 0/6 after /taskinfo returned “File not found” and a test expecting HTTP 405 failed. In address-book-jakarta-to-quarkus, GPT-6 Astra + Codex scored 2/10 after list and create pages returned HTTP 404. Source-framework wiring surviving into the target: In cargotracker-jakarta-to-spring, Gemini 3.8 Flash + mini-swe retained JSF/JoinFaces wiring in the Spring Boot target, which then failed during startup while creating a facesContext bean. Packaging incompatible with the target runtime: In cart-spring-to-jakarta, GPT-6 Astra + Codex reached a deployment failure because the packaging type left by the migration was not supported by the target Liberty runtime. These failures illustrate why ScarfBench validates beyond compilation: Nearly three in four classified failures in this evaluation appeared at runtime. Agent efficiency reveals different operating profiles On the 200 tasks remaining after the four-task sensitivity exclusion, Claude Opus 5 + Claude Code used the fewest median turns at 32. GPT-6.1 Sol + Codex used 36, Gemma 4 26B-A4B + mini-swe 40, Gemini 4 Argon + Antigravity 42, GPT-6 Astra + Codex 45, Kimi K3 + kimi-code 47, Qwen 3.8 Max + qwen-code and Gemini 3.1 Pro + OpenHands 53, Claude Opus 5.5 + Claude Code 64, and Gemini 3.8 Flash + mini-swe 79. Where harness-reported cost was available — for the Claude Code, Codex, mini-swe and kimi-code harnesses; the Antigravity, qwen-code and OpenHands harnesses did not emit per-run cost — the configurations showed distinct cost profiles: Model / harness Median turns Turns, successful runs Cost / successful run Cost per solved task Claude Opus 5 / Claude Code 32 30 $1.76 $3.83 Claude Opus 5.5 / Claude Code 64 60 $5.98 $10.10 GPT-6.1 Sol / Codex 36 34 $0.64 $1.25 GPT-6 Astra / Codex 45 44 $3.55 $6.65 Gemini 3.8 Flash / mini-swe 79 74 $0.73 $1.59 Kimi K3 / kimi-code 47 44 $1.27 $3.21 IBM and Kaggle are building a living ScarfBench leaderboard The latest ScarfBench evaluation is also the start of a deeper collaboration between IBM and Kaggle. The two teams bring complementary strengths: IBM developed ScarfBench around enterprise Java modernization, while Kaggle brings independent evaluation infrastructure and long-term leaderboard maintenance. The collaboration is intended to make the benchmark reproducible outside its original development environment and useful as new model-and-agent configurations are released. The collaboration has three concrete parts. First, Kaggle consulted with IBM on the rigorous design of the benchmark and evaluation. Second, Kaggle independently reproduced and ran the evaluation on its platform and sponsored the compute. Third, Kaggle will maintain the benchmark long-term and add new models as they are released. The ScarfBench leaderboard provides the public view of these results. Public model submission is not available at launch but is on the roadmap. What we have learned so far ScarfBench was built around the demanding premise that coding agents participating meaningfully in enterprise modernization need to be evaluated on the outcome enterprises ultimately care about: working software. The latest evaluation reinforces that premise. Leading configurations can compile nearly every task in the sensitivity set, but compilation hides a harder problem. Routes disappear, HTTP behavior changes, source-framework wiring survives migrations, applications fail during startup, and business behavior diverges from the expected system. That gap between code that builds and software that works is where ScarfBench is most informative. As new model/harness combinations arrive, a maintained benchmark can show whether progress comes from better generated changes, more effective debugging and iteration, more efficient tool use, or a combination of these capabilities.

blogs.name: IBM Research Blog
blogs.title: PyTorch opens the AI ecosystem to a new class of accelerators
blogs.author: Peter Hess
blogs.description: IBM has made Spyre a first-class PyTorch backend, giving developers the same workflows across devices.
blogs.content: In October 2025, IBM and the PyTorch Foundation outlined a plan for deeper Spyre enablement in 2026: treating the accelerator as a first-class PyTorch backend and supporting multi-accelerator scheduling. The latest software ecosystem updates deliver on that promise. Together, torch-spyre, Spyre's vLLM plugin, compiler improvements, and continuous integration work are making it easier to bring familiar models and workflows to a different class of AI hardware. AI is increasingly being embedded in the systems that process transactions, detect fraud, analyze claims, and assist employees. And with this growing usage, the AI hardware ecosystem is expanding. GPUs remain central to modern AI, but they are increasingly joined by accelerators with different architectures, execution models, and performance characteristics. Giving developers more choices requires more than building new chips. The software ecosystem must make new accelerators usable without forcing developers to abandon familiar models, tools, and workflows. Spyre is IBM’s dataflow AI accelerator, optimized for inference. It is designed for enterprise teams running AI alongside their applications and data on IBM Z, LinuxONE, and Power systems. Its reduced-precision compute is well suited to the matrix-heavy work in language generation and embedding models. Unlike a conventional GPU, which executes kernels as instruction streams across scheduled groups of threads, Spyre triggers computation as data arrives at its compute engines. PyTorch provides the common layer that allows this different architecture to participate in an ecosystem built largely around GPUs. Extending PyTorch beyond GPUs At the center of this effort is torch-spyre , a PyTorch backend that compiles ordinary PyTorch code into an executable plan for Spyre. Most of a model’s logic passes through the PyTorch compiler unchanged. When a model contains an operation that the underlying stack cannot yet lower effectively, an adapter can replace it with a mathematically equivalent form that the compiler can handle. The model’s computation remains the same, while its implementation becomes compatible with the accelerator. The move to PyTorch’s Inductor backend also reduced the amount of custom compiler code that the team must maintain. The resulting compiler is roughly seven times smaller than the system it replaced and measurably less complex per function. That smaller surface area makes it easier to carry improvements from upstream PyTorch into torch-spyre and focus Spyre-specific work where it matters. The same principle applies at the device boundary. In a recent demonstration , moving graph construction off the data-transfer path improved Granite 3.3 8B performance at batch size 1 and sequence length 1024 by 9.9% for prefill and 13.6% for decode. Removing that work from compute dispatch as well brought the total improvement to 1.7 times faster prefill and 2.4 times faster decode, with roughly three quarters of the gain coming from the compute path. Preserving vLLM portability Spyre is an out-of-tree accelerator , rather than one of the GPU platforms most commonly supported by AI software. Spyre relies on TorchDynamo to trace a model graph and TorchInductor to lower that graph into representations optimized for the target hardware. Within vLLM, extension mechanisms such as CustomOp and PluggableLayer allow a hardware plugin to customize behavior without reimplementing large portions of the software stack. Preserving these extension points matters as vLLM evolves. Some new model implementations are becoming increasingly specialized for particular models and frontier GPU hardware. To preserve portability alongside that optimization work, the vLLM community is developing hardware-agnostic layers that are isolated from hardware-specific paths and designed to be compilable, extensible, and portable across accelerator platforms. Early support has landed in vLLM, and the pathway has been validated with the Spyre plugin on models including Gemma 4, Qwen3, and Granite 4.2. On NVIDIA H100 GPUs, these hardware-agnostic layers delivered total token throughput within 3.4% of the native implementation, measured as the geometric mean across three recent models. One workflow, more hardware choices For IBM Z, LinuxONE, and Power11 users, the intended experience is straightforward: Obtain models from ecosystems like Hugging Face and use substantially the same PyTorch-based workflows they would use with Nvidia GPUs. Shared PyTorch extension points hide much of the architectural difference beneath the framework, reducing adoption friction and avoiding an experience limited to a small catalog of specially packaged model weights. Consider an insurance-claims workflow that combines XGBoost models for fraud detection with a Gemma 26B model on Spyre for forensic analysis. The software stack enables developers to assemble the workflow using familiar model ecosystems and framework interfaces, while the hardware is chosen for the work it suits. Spyre's PyTorch integration is also how it connects to llm-d . llm-d runs distributed inference on top of vLLM and is built to support multiple accelerator types, not a single hardware path. vLLM reaches each accelerator through PyTorch: Once a device has a working PyTorch backend, a vLLM hardware plugin can expose it, and then llm-d can schedule work onto it. Spyre follows this path. torch-spyre provides the PyTorch backend, and the Spyre vLLM plugin builds on top of it. As a result, the work that makes Spyre a PyTorch device is the same work that makes it usable in llm-d deployments. Making compatibility measurable Broad compatibility is only useful when users have clear evidence that models run reliably across platforms. IBM Research engineers are building that evidence through end-to-end model testing and continuous integration. This work helps the team detect when upstream framework changes affect downstream hardware support . End-to-end model testing is critical because failures can arise from combinations of operations, shapes, layouts, numerical ranges, and compiler fusion behavior that isolated unit tests do not reveal. Running real models against trusted CPU or GPU references turns each model into both a compatibility test and a probe for hardening the platform. It also gives developers clearer signals about which models and accelerator configurations have been exercised together. In the second half of 2026, IBM, Red Hat, and their collaborators in the PyTorch Foundation including Meta and Hugging Face have pushed new software ecosystem updates covering day-one model enablement, hardware-agnostic models in vLLM, continuous regression and release testing, and native-device integration. A new demonstration on the frontend and backend compiler explains more of the stack . Together, this body of work shows how model adapters, compiler paths, runtime integration, vLLM extensions, and CI/CD combine to support Spyre as a first-class participant in the PyTorch ecosystem. By combining familiar workflows, portable compiler paths, broad model enablement, and transparent validation, IBM is helping make hardware choice a practical option rather than a software integration burden.

blogs.description: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro, our most capable 3T-class open-weight model with 1M-token context and major advances in coding, 3D modeling, and financial research.
blogs.content: Scroll to explore Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro We're introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro , the first model in our new K3.1 series and our most capable 3T-class open-weight model to date, with a 1-million-token context window. It delivers substantial improvements across coding, 3D creation, financial research, and other agentic capabilities. We are also releasing Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed , which delivers 2-3× the speed of K3.1 Pro for more responsive interactions. Kimi K3.1 Pro and Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed are available today on Kimi.ai , Kimi Work , Kimi Code , and the Kimi API . The full model weights will be released by Nov 4. Advancing the Frontier of Open Intelligence Kimi K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3, with substantially larger post-training compute. To enable large-scale joint RL across hundreds of downstream domains , we optimized every layer of the stack — the RL framework, long-context inference, training efficiency, sandbox infrastructure, rollout scheduling, and a shared platform for environment quality checks — so that each increment of RL compute delivers stable, predictable returns. As a result, K3.1 Pro achieves consistent gains in every domain. Across coding, agentic, and knowledge benchmarks, K3.1 Pro matches or approaches the strongest proprietary models. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 , which evaluates coding agents on realistic, resource-constrained terminal tasks using strict task-specific tests, K3.1 Pro scores 65.7%, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (58.2%) and narrowly behind Claude Opus 5.5 (66.4%) . And on Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon , our internal benchmark that tests coding agents' multi-step execution, tool use, and end-to-end problem solving across diverse engineering domains, K3.1 Pro scores 61.2% , above K3's 55.95% . Coding K3.1 Pro covers the full range of coding work, from quick fixes in real codebases to full-project builds. It also brings a more considered visual style to games and web experiences, and knows how to build them with the right tools. K3.1 Pro works effectively across game engines such as Unity, Unreal Engine, and Godot , combining them with web search and 3D generation to create complete experiences. Its front-end pages, interactive Three.js scenes, and 3D assets show stronger composition, typography, animation, and polish. The examples below were created end to end by K3.1 Pro: K3.1 Pro's long-horizon coding capabilities are also strengthened through large-scale reinforcement learning. In one internal test, it built a human walking dynamics simulator with integrated training and evaluation pipelines on top of human-atlas , an open-source anatomical model of the human body comprising 296 skeletal components, including cartilage, and 402 muscle components. Across 167 missions and 420 independent reviews, it analyzed experimental results, diagnosed problems, and iteratively refined the walking controller, enabling the simulated human to go from collapsing within seconds to walking continuously with alternating strides for 11.2 seconds. When reward shaping failed to improve arm motion, K3.1 Pro did not simply keep adjusting the reward: it ran open-loop probes of the simulator's dynamics, identified and corrected 36 errors in shoulder-muscle moment-arm calculations, and then retrained the controller. 3D Modeling and Design K3.1 Pro is strong at 3D creation and spatial reasoning. On BenchCAD , which tests 3D reconstruction from multi-view renderings through CAD code generation, K3.1 Pro scores 92.7% with tools , approaching the performance of Claude Opus 5.5 (96.2%) and GPT-6 Astra (95.9%) . From a text brief, sketch, or reference image, it can infer shape, proportions, and spatial relationships to create usable 3D models. It also has a stronger grasp of existing asset libraries and model collections. K3.1 Pro particularly excels at parametric modeling, from mechanical parts and architectural models to configurable products and custom furniture. Without MCP connectors, it can write and run scripts for tools like Blender and CAD software to build and refine assets, edit components, and adjust geometry, materials, and scene layout. Below are examples of 3D assets K3.1 Pro created for brand films, games, and interactive web experiences: 3D Make is now live on kimi.ai and the Kimi app — preview and edit your 3D models online, download them ready for 3D printing, or export them as videos or Live Photos to share anywhere. Finance With stronger reasoning and agentic capability, K3.1 Pro is capable of end-to-end delivery of complete financial workflows. K3.1 Pro achieves state-of-the-art results on OfficeQA Pro v2 (64.4), which tests complex fiscal data analysis over real financial documents through retrieval, cross-document verification, and multi-step numerical reasoning. K3.1 Pro also improves over K3 on Frontier Finance, which measures support for complete investment workflows from screening to profitability analysis. K3.1 Pro also improves significantly across all our internal finance benchmarks: Financial Modeling evaluates formula linkage, financial logic, and final workbook quality in real-world modeling tasks. K3.1 Pro improves on K3 by 7.2 points. Financial Research evaluates whether models can produce auditable research under evidence and cutoff constraints. K3.1 Pro improves on K3 by 11.6 points. Business Operation evaluates long-horizon management and decision-making in a simulated business environment. K3.1 Pro achieves about 4.2× K3's performance. Financial analysis and investment research demand a high degree of factual accuracy. To address this, we made targeted improvements to K3.1 Pro's factual accuracy on real-world tasks and challenging prompts. On Kimi Hallu Bench Hard bench, an internal benchmark designed to stress-test factual accuracy, its claim-level hallucination rate fell from 23.4% for K3 to 8.3%, while the share of responses containing at least one factual error was just 42.4% of its predecessor's rate. (The evaluation is a stress test for factual accuracy, with examples deliberately crafted to probe situations where models are prone to errors. The reported rates do not represent overall error rates in daily use.) The cases below show how K3.1 Pro handles financial modeling, investment analysis, and source-grounded research in practice: Cybersecurity As K3.1 Pro became more capable, we spent a correspondingly larger share of our effort understanding where cyber capability comes from, and how much of it we can control. We therefore analyzed and evaluated K3.1 Pro's vulnerability research capabilities, and applied targeted controls during training to reduce potential misuse risk while preserving general usefulness. Identifying and removing cyber-related data. During development, we observed vulnerability research performance improving steadily as post-training scaled. Tracing the source of this trend, we found that cyber-related content was embedded within the general mid-training corpus, and cyber-related tasks were present in the RL environment mix — a natural byproduct of training on broad data. In preliminary experiments on internal models, we found that without data removal at either the mid-training or the RL stage, downstream cyber capability would increase substantially. These findings gave us a concrete lever for control. For the open-weight release of K3.1 Pro, we identified and removed cyber-related data from both training stages, while retaining the general-purpose coding tasks needed for model usefulness. We will continue to apply appropriate controls at every training stage, of which cyber-related data identification and restriction is one example. Evaluation and results. After data cleaning, we evaluated K3.1 Pro on xdev-bench-hard, our in-house benchmark of expert-curated, source-code-based vulnerability discovery and exploitation tasks, calibrated to provide meaningful differentiation at our current capability level. Most tasks faithfully reproduce recently disclosed vulnerabilities in software such as the Linux kernel, Node.js, JavaScriptCore, Exim, and VirGL, with mitigations enabled. Each task provides the vulnerable source code, a short bug hint, and the corresponding binary; the agent must develop an exploit, achieve arbitrary code execution in a separate sandbox, and retrieve a secret string for automated verification. We report pass@3 over a random subset of runs, with no hard timeouts or output token limits. On xdev-bench-hard, the checkpoint without these risk-reduction measures — no cyber-related data removal at mid-training and no cyber-related RL environment filtering — solves 90.5% of problems at pass@3; the final K3.1 Pro reaches 81.0%. The comparison shows that data removal meaningfully reduces cyber capability relative to what the same training pipeline would otherwise produce. At the same time, K3.1 Pro improves substantially over its predecessor, indicating that stronger general coding and long-horizon debugging capabilities generalize to cyber tasks even after targeted data removal. K3.1 Pro's cyber capability remains behind that of frontier proprietary models that have been publicly available for at least three months. We will keep evolving our internal benchmarks so that evaluation stays informative as model capabilities continue to advance. Open-weight principles. These evaluations frame our open-weight release decision. First, we aim not to release open weights that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability. K3.1 Pro's offensive cyber capability is, by design, below what our pipeline can produce, and remains behind that of frontier proprietary models. Second, we intend to progressively raise the cyber capability available in open weights. We believe making K3.1 Pro available in a non-discriminatory way benefits people who need dual-use capabilities for defensive purposes. When a capable model is open and runs on infrastructure its users control, many more teams gain the means to audit the code they maintain — including legacy systems that rarely receive dedicated security reviews. We believe that letting this capability diffuse gradually — rather than concentrating it in a few proprietary systems — ultimately makes all software more secure. Availability Kimi K3.1 Pro rolls out today across the Kimi product family: on Kimi.ai and the Kimi mobile apps, Kimi Work and Kimi Code, and through the Kimi API . Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026. Kimi Enterprise administrators can enable K3.1 Pro for their organization; access is off by default at launch. Details for each channel: Kimi Agents: Download or update to the latest Kimi app from your mobile app store, available on iOS, Android, and HarmonyOS, or visit kimi.ai . Work with Kimi K3.1 Pro: Download the latest Kimi Work desktop app , version 3.1.0 or later, available for Windows and Apple silicon Macs. Code with Kimi K3.1 Pro: Run Kimi Code and select Kimi K3.1 Pro using the /model command. Build with the Kimi API: Visit the Kimi API Platform and select kimi-k3.1-pro / kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed. Zero Data Retention is available for API customers. Bring Kimi to your organization: Kimi Business provides enterprise-grade data privacy and member management, with complete separation between personal and organization accounts. Visit the pricing page and select “Get Kimi Business” to subscribe for your team. Benchmarks Footnotes Unless otherwise specified, all Kimi K3.1 Pro results reported below are obtained with the reasoning effort set to 'max', temperature = 1.0, and top-p = 0.95. Coding benchmarks Terminal-Bench 4.0. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the Claude-Code harness. The DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 is taken from the release blog ( https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 ). All remaining scores are taken as the maximum value reported in either their blog posts or the official Terminal-Bench 4.0 leaderboard ( https://www.tbench.ai/ ). Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the Claude-Code harness. Our internal evaluation of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 yields a score of 9.3; However, an older version, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, scores 15.7 on the official Terminal-Bench-Science, so we report 15.7 here; all remaining scores are from the official Terminal-Bench-Science leaderboard ( https://www.terminal-bench-science.ai/ ). DeepSWE v1.1. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the Claude-Code harness. All scores are taken from each model's respective technical report. GPT-6 Astra( https://openai.com/index/gpt-6-astra/ ). Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1( https://www.anthropic.com/claude-opus-5-5-system-card and https://www.anthropic.com/claude-fable-5-1-mythos-5-1-system-card ); DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 ( https://api-docs.deepseek.com/news/news261017/ ); GLM-5.3 ( https://z.ai/blog/glm-5.3 ). SWE-Marathon v1.1. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the Claude-Code harness. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 is evaluated with the ClaudeCode harness. All other scores are taken from the official SWE-Marathon leaderboard ( https://www.swe-marathon.org/ ). PostTrainBench. Kimi K3.1 Pro and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 were evaluated internally on v1.2 using the Claude-Code harness and H20 GPUs instead of H100 GPUs. For stable evaluation, all judge models used DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 at maximum effort, which best matched the official GPT-5.6-Terra (xhigh) judge in testing. Other scores are from the official leaderboard ( https://posttrainbench.com/ ). ProgramBench (binary score). We report binary scores rather than raw ProgramBench scores: a task receives a score of 1 if its ProgramBench score is ≥95%, and 0 otherwise. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the Claude-Code harness. The DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 and GLM-5.3 scores are taken from the release blog ( https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 ); all remaining scores are from the Vals ProgramBench leaderboard ( https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/programbench ). Internal Coding Bench: Kimi Code Bench 2.0 and Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with Claude-Code harnesses; All other models are evaluated at their max-effort setting. Note that proprietary model testing may involve some fallback behavior. BenchCAD. Open models are evaluated by us on 1,000-case subsets randomly sampled from the full 17,900-case Vision2Code dataset, at maximum reasoning effort. With-tools results use the Claude Code harness; without-tools results use single-shot generation with the official BenchCAD prompts and scoring pipeline. Scores for Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 are taken from the Claude Opus 5.5 System Card ; GPT‑6 Astra’s with-tools score is taken from its official report . GPT‑6 Astra has not reported a without-tools score and is marked “—”. Agentic benchmarks BioMysteryBench dataset is drawn from the official v11 release , with Kimi K3 as the judge model. We evaluate Kimi K3.1 Pro with Kimi Code, GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 with Claude Code, and GPT-6 Astra with Codex. Scores for the Claude models are taken directly from their official system cards. Our Agents’ Last Exam dataset is drawn from the official v1.1 release , comprising 122 tasks, including 86 CLI tasks, with environment images aligned with the official Hugging Face release. We additionally assign a score of zero to runs that bypass the task’s stated requirements, such as retrieving answers online instead of performing the required analysis in Wireshark. DeepSeek and Kimi are evaluated using Claude Code and Kimi Code, respectively. All other results are taken from the official benchmark website. OfficeQA Pro, OfficeQA Pro v2. GPT-6 Astra is evaluated with Codex, while all other models are evaluated with Claude Code. Each task provides the agent with the entire PDF corpus, with all PDFs rendered as images and no machine-readable text available. We observed instances in the trajectories of certain external models where they retrieved reference answers online; Consequently, we assigned a score of zero to these tasks. Frontier Finance is evaluated with the official finance agent v2 harness. HANDBOOK.md is evaluated using the official harness built on OpenHands, with evaluation tasks drawn from the benchmark’s early open-source v1 release. Harvey Legal Agent is evaluated on a public dataset of 1,251 tasks using Artificial Analysis’s Stirrup harness, with performance reported as the all-pass rate (i.e., the percentage of tasks that pass all rubric criteria). OSWorld V2.1 is evaluated with the Kimi Agent harness in the official OSWorld v2 repo, while GPT-6 Astra's score is taken from Muse Wonder's technical report. DECK-Arena evaluates presentation generation on real-world queries, while Design Bench covers graphic design via direct and reference-image few-shot prompting; Both run models across python-pptx, pptxjs, and Kimi's in-house DSL in a harness with integrated search and image generation, using an automated grader calibrated on 10,000+ human judgments. MCP Atlas. All models are evaluated on the 500-task public subset with a 100-turn limit, using Gemini 3.1 Pro as the judge. BrowseComp. We adopt the context-compaction strategy used in the Claude model cards, triggered at 200K tokens. We allow a maximum of 500 steps; if this limit is reached before a task is completed, we force the agent to provide an answer, which is then judged. All BrowseComp runs are conducted with temperature=1.0 and top-p=1.0. GDPval-AA v2.1, AA-Briefcase v1.1 and AutomationBench-AA scores are cited from https://artificialanalysis.ai/ , Apex Agents scores are cited from https://www.mercor.com/apex/apex-agents-leaderboard/ GDP.pdf w/ python, ZeroBench w/ python and ChartoGraphy w/ python are averaged over five runs. Other multimodal benchmarks (w/ python) are averaged over four runs. For GDP.pdf w/ python: Each original PDF file is sent to the sandbox, where the model can use IPython tool to process it. Final responses are graded against each rubric criterion using Gemini-3.5-Flash (medium reasoning effort) and the official judging prompt. We report the task-macro mean rubric pass rate: for each task, we average the fraction of rubric criteria passed over five independent runs, then average these task-level scores equally across all tasks. Reasoning & Knowledge & Multimodal benchmarks GDP.pdf. Each PDF is provided as page images resized to a longest edge of 1,152 pixels, interleaved with Docling-extracted text in page order. Responses are graded against each rubric criterion using Gemini-3.5-Flash Medium and the official judging prompt. We report the strict pass rate among fully scored responses. HLE and HLE-Diamond evaluate general knowledge and reasoning capabilities. We report accuracy on the full evaluation sets, with 2,500 questions for HLE and 1,000 questions for HLE-Diamond. For models marked with an asterisk (*), accuracy is reported on the text-only subset of questions. GDP.pdf, ZeroBench and ChartoGraphy are averaged over five runs. Other multimodal benchmarks are averaged over four runs. GDP.pdf scores of GLM-5.3 Max and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 Max is cited from https://artificialanalysis.ai/ . MMMU-Pro is evaluated following the official protocol, preserving the original input order and prepending images to the text input. Kimi Hallucination Benchmark evaluates factual accuracy on an internal set of challenging, de-identified prompts drawn from practical work tasks. We report the claim-level hallucination rate assessed by fact-checking agents. Cybersecurity benchmarks ExploitBench. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the official ExploitBench harness under the 300-turn budget. We report the pass@5 max capability score: for each environment, the best run across 5 seeds, scored by the number of capability flags reached out of 16, where achieving arbitrary code execution counts as achieving all 16 capabilities. The GPT-6 Astra score is taken from https://openai.com/index/gpt-6-astra/ ; the Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Mythos 5.1 scores are taken from https://www.anthropic.com/claude-opus-5-5-system-card ; the GLM-5.3 score is taken from https://z.ai/blog/glm-5.3 . ExploitGym. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the KimiCode harness under a 6-hour wall-clock budget per task. The GPT-6 Astra score is taken from https://openai.com/index/gpt-6-astra/ ; the Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Mythos 5.1 scores are taken from https://www.anthropic.com/claude-opus-5-5-system-card at the 6-hour budget; the GLM-5.3 score is taken from https://z.ai/blog/glm-5.3 . xdev-Bench-hard: Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the KimiCode harness. GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 are evaluated with the Claude Code harness. Try K3.1 Pro
